headline: High: TREK’s browser/MCP and xonsh’s shell/filesystem overlap creates dangerous default pathways for prompt injection, data leakage, and cascading errors.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: TREK can run browsers and use MCP, so it may ingest external or tool-mediated content; xonsh reads stdin/stdout and executes shell expressions, creating a plausible bridge if TREK output is copied or piped into it. No direct shared channel is documented, so this is inferred rather than observed.
conditions: IF TREK output is copied into xonsh stdin or shell commands
IF an MCP tool returns attacker-controlled text that xonsh later executes
mitigations: Disable copy-paste from browser outputs into shell sessions
Require manual review before any TREK-generated text is executed
Use separate terminals and accounts for the two agents
Add a prompt-injection filter on MCP outputs
requires-engineering: enforce provenance tags on all cross-agent text

B_data_leakage.rationale: TREK touches API keys, MFA secrets, reservations, and email addresses, while xonsh has broad filesystem read/write plus broad network egress. If they share a workspace or files, xonsh can exfiltrate sensitive TREK data; the profiles do not show isolation between their file surfaces, so uncertainty pushes upward.
conditions: IF both agents can access the same directory or mounted volume
IF TREK stores secrets or reservations in files that xonsh can read
mitigations: Place each agent in a separate filesystem namespace
Remove secrets from any shared directory
Rotate exposed API keys and MFA secrets
Restrict xonsh network egress to approved destinations
requires-engineering: add per-file access controls and audit logs

C_capability_conflict.rationale: TREK supports real-time collaborative sessions and multiple instances, while xonsh can write the filesystem and spawn subprocesses. They do not both advertise git modification, but overlapping write access to shared files or state can still cause conflicts in default collaborative setups.
conditions: IF both agents write to the same workspace or database files
IF TREK sessions and xonsh processes run concurrently against shared state
mitigations: Assign separate working directories
Serialize writes with a lock file
Disable concurrent edits during xonsh runs
Back up shared files before each session
requires-engineering: add transactional locking around shared resources

D_cascading_error.rationale: TREK is described as a real-time collaborative travel planner with AI built in, and xonsh can execute shell commands and subprocesses. If xonsh treats TREK output as authoritative, planning errors can cascade into incorrect commands or file changes; no verification step is documented.
conditions: IF xonsh consumes TREK-generated plans or commands without validation
IF TREK output is used to drive shell automation
mitigations: Require human approval before executing TREK-derived commands
Validate TREK outputs against a schema
Log and diff all generated commands before execution
Use dry-run mode for shell actions
requires-engineering: add automated consistency checks between planner and executor

E_compliance.rationale: TREK handles user accounts, email addresses, confirmation numbers, API keys, and MFA secrets, while xonsh touches filesystem contents and environment variables with broad egress. That combination creates a plausible compliance mismatch for sensitive travel data if both process the same records; no residency or retention controls are documented, so uncertainty remains.
conditions: IF regulated personal data or secrets are stored in files accessible to xonsh
IF retention or residency requirements apply to TREK records
mitigations: Keep regulated data out of shared filesystems
Minimize logged fields in TREK and xonsh
Review retention settings before processing sensitive records
Restrict xonsh egress for regulated datasets
requires-engineering: document residency and retention boundaries
